The spot premium for imported cathode has remained unchanged at $40-60/t in the past two weeks; whist the premium for SXEW cathode was also unchanged at $35-45/t. We expect the spot market to remain quiet before year’s end, as we have heard that banks have tightened the issuance of letters of credit needed for trading in imported cathode and western market participants will be out of the market for the holiday season in the western world. In the past week, domestic cathode prices have given back some of their gains as the minor rally in prices that started mid-November has started to reverse in line with movements in the LME price. We estimate that the stocks we monitor in China fell to 985,357t by 21st December 2012, down from 1,001,901t two weeks ago. Stocks in Shanghai bonded warehouses remained unchanged at around 750,000t-800,000t, but we have heard of a fall in Guangdong stock levels, therefore we have adjusted down our estimate of stocks in bonded warehouses in Guangdong to 50,000t from 75,000t. This is in line with what we are hearing about downstream users restocking, as Guangdong stocks track physical demand more closely than Shanghai stocks. China’s year-to-date total cathode imports have risen significantly compared to the same period in 2011, up around 30% y-o-y between Jan-Nov 2012, an increase of 730,000t taking imports to 3.16Mt. When coupled with the 10% y-o-y rise in domestic production of cathode, and the lower 5% y-o-y growth in © 2012 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 5 **December 2012** www.crugroup.com consumption, we can see that the majority of the increased imports ended up in bonded warehouses of Shanghai. Since the beginning of January 2012, we estimate that cathode stocks in the bonded area of Shanghai have risen by 500,000t to between 750,000-800,000t. In 2013, we think that cathode stock levels in Shanghai bonded warehouses may remain unchanged, or rise slighlty from the current level. We also expect imports to decline slighlty in 2013 from the levels we have seen this year. This is because we have heard that the majority of Chinese buyers have reduced the amount of cathode they are going to buy through annual contracts in 2013. However, we expect some of the decline in imports on annual contracts to be offset by continued copper financing demand, which will remain strong due to the interest rate differential between borrowing in US dollars and borrowing in Renminbi. # China cuts tax on highly purified catho

de export 

China’s Ministry of Finance announced its 2013 changes to import and export taxes on 17<sup>th</sup> December, adjusting the import/export taxes of many goods, including the export of some cathode.  The 5% export tax on highly purifiied cathode, with Cu content of at least 99.9999%, will be removed from August. However, the export tax on other highly purified cathode, with Cu content higher than 99.9935% but lower than 99.9999%, was left unchanged at 5%.  The export tax on normal commercial-use cathode, with Cu content of 99.95%, was also left unchanged at 10%.  The seven Chinese smelters who are qualified for copper tolling can from August enjoy 0% export taxes when importing copper concentrate and exporting highly purified cathode, however, they will still pay the 14% VAT. In spite of this, we think this policy will have very little effect on the market or copper exports in the short run as the production of highly purifiied cathode requires more technology and has high associated costs. Additionally, the premiums for such highly purified cathode are higher than normal commercial-use cathode, meaning its liquidity is not as good and that it is more difficult to sell. 

# More postive macro news 

Since our last CCF, the macro news out of China, and external measures such as the US Fed embarking on QE4, look supportive for copper demand.  The latest HSBC/Markit China flash PMI for the first part of December rose to 50.9, a 14 month high.  At the same time the Chinese central government has given some positive signals at its central economic meeting, which took place on the15<sup>th</sup> - 16<sup>th</sup> December, and is believed to set the tone for the coming year’s economic plans. 

The Chinese government reiterated its aim to enlarge domestic demand in 2013, and during a press conference held by the Ministry of Commerce (Mofcom) on 18<sup>th</sup> December, senior government official mentioned the slow-down of growth in the home appliance and autos sector.  This suggests the government may launch more supporting policies for these two industries which could involve subsidies for the purchase of environmentally friendly and energy-saving cars, as well as for other white goods such as washing machines and air-conditioners. 

In 2013, we expect China’s general macro environment to improve from 2012, as the government reiterated plans to promote urbanisation which could create more demand in the real estate sector as well

# The limits of government investment 

Next year will be the third year of China’s current Five Year Plan, with investment being driv

en by the long run targets set out in 2011.  Significant amounts of copper intensive investment are still in the pipeline but the 2013 targets for areas like social housing are not as ambitious as the past two years. 

The construction and furnishing of social housing is relatively copper intensive and will be supportive of copper demand across the whole period 2011-2015.  However, the central government plans to start construction of fewer units in 2013, with a target of 5M units of social housing down from 7M units this year.  If targets are met this year, the total amount of social housing completed or under construction will reach 22M by the end of 2013.  This implies that the government would still need to build 14M units in the years 2014-15, providing a boost to copper demand at the end of the 12<sup>th</sup> Five Year Plan. 

A second area of investment with more potential to stimulate copper demand is railway investment, which was subdued for part of 2012 following the 2011 Wenzhou high-speed train crash.  According to the European copper institute, the construction of high-speed railway uses 10t of copper per kilometre of track.  The government’s plans are for the total amount of high-speed railway track in China to reach 18,000km by the end of 2015, an increase of 13,000km from the end of the 11th five year plan (end of 2010).  Thus far only 5,000km out of the additional 13,000km railway tracks has been completed, meaning the rate of railway construction will need to rise marginally in the second half of the plan. Although the official budget for the ministry of railways is due to increase only moderately next year to RMB 53bn from RMB51.6bn (US$8.4bn from US$8.2bn), the ministry is free to raise its own funding and has upped its budget three times in the past year, therefore there is potential for this to rise over the course of the year. 

Owing to the government’s efforts to rebalance the economy, government led copper intensive stimulus packages are not expected.  However, the government spending plans will provide some support to copper demand out to 2015 with targeted infrastructure continued to be built as the government pushes urbanisation.
